overview: A temporary view registers a DataFrame under a name so it can be queried with SQL via `spark.sql(...)`, bridging the DataFrame and SQL APIs without writing data anywhere.

`createOrReplaceTempView` creates a SESSION-scoped view visible only within the SparkSession that created it, whereas `createGlobalTempView` creates a CLUSTER-wide view stored in the special `global_temp` database and shareable across SparkSessions of the same application.

Temporary views are lazy and NOT materialized: they store the DataFrame's logical plan (a query definition), not its data, and their lifecycle is tied to the SparkSession (or the application, for global views).
learningObjectives: Differentiate `createOrReplaceTempView` (session scope) from `createGlobalTempView` (global_temp / application scope) and know how to query each.
Understand that temporary views are lazy logical-plan references -- not materialized tables -- and are recomputed on each query.
Master the lifecycle of temporary views and how it is tied to the SparkSession or application, plus how to drop them.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A temporary view is a named reference to a DataFrame's logical plan in the Spark catalog that can be queried via Spark SQL. `createOrReplaceTempView(name)` registers a session-local view scoped to the creating SparkSession. `createGlobalTempView(name)` registers a view in the reserved `global_temp` database, scoped to the SparkApplication and accessible from any SparkSession sharing the same SparkContext. Neither persists data nor a definition to the metastore; both are in-memory catalog entries that disappear when their scope ends.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A temporary view is like giving a nickname to a DataFrame so you can talk to it in SQL. A session temp view (createOrReplaceTempView) is a private nickname only your current Spark session knows. A global temp view (createGlobalTempView) is a shared nickname that every session in the same application can use, but you must call it by its full name `global_temp.thatname`. Importantly, the nickname points to the recipe (the query), not a saved copy of the data -- Spark re-runs the recipe each time you query it.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early Spark used `registerTempTable` on SchemaRDD/DataFrame. With the unified Dataset/DataFrame API and SparkSession in Spark 2.0, `registerTempTable` was deprecated in favor of `createOrReplaceTempView`. Spark 2.1 introduced global temporary views (`createGlobalTempView`) and the reserved `global_temp` database to allow sharing temporary views across sessions within an application -- useful in multi-session contexts like notebooks and shared Spark applications.

whyItMatters.business: Temporary views let analysts and engineers reuse familiar SQL on Spark DataFrames, accelerating ad-hoc analysis and report development without persisting intermediate tables.
whyItMatters.engineering: They cleanly mix the DataFrame and SQL APIs, enabling complex pipelines to be expressed in whichever style is clearer per step, with no I/O to manage or clean up.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because views are just logical-plan references, they add no storage and let Catalyst optimize the full combined query; but being non-materialized means repeated queries recompute, which can be costly at scale.
whyItMatters.cost: No data is written, so there is no storage cost, but unaware reuse of a heavy view recomputes upstream work each query -- understanding laziness avoids surprise compute bills.
whyItMatters.reliability: Scope and lifecycle awareness prevents bugs like a view vanishing when a session ends or name clashes across sessions; global vs session scope choices affect correctness in multi-session apps.

coreComponents.name: createOrReplaceTempView (session view)
coreComponents.definition: Registers or replaces a session-scoped temporary view referencing a DataFrame's logical plan.
coreComponents.purpose: Make a DataFrame queryable via SQL within the current SparkSession.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Add/replace an entry in the session-local temporary view catalog; the name is unqualified and visible only to the creating session.

coreComponents.name: createGlobalTempView (global view)
coreComponents.definition: Registers a temporary view in the reserved `global_temp` database, scoped to the SparkApplication and visible to all sessions sharing the SparkContext.
coreComponents.purpose: Share a temporary view across multiple SparkSessions within the same application.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Add an entry under `global_temp`; queries must reference it as `global_temp.<name>`. It throws if the name already exists (use createOrReplaceGlobalTempView to overwrite).

coreComponents.name: spark.sql + catalog lifecycle
coreComponents.definition: The SQL entry point that resolves view names against the catalog, plus the catalog methods to inspect and drop views.
coreComponents.purpose: Execute SQL against registered views and manage their lifecycle.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Resolve unqualified names against the session catalog and `global_temp.<name>` against the global catalog; drop views via `catalog.dropTempView` / `dropGlobalTempView`.

internalWorking: When you call createOrReplaceTempView, Spark stores the DataFrame's analyzed logical plan in the SessionCatalog's in-memory temporary-view map under the given name -- no data is copied or written.

A `spark.sql("SELECT ... FROM viewname")` parses the SQL, looks up `viewname` in the catalog, and substitutes the view's logical plan into the query, after which Catalyst optimizes the combined plan as if you had written it inline.
Because only the plan is stored, each query that references the view re-executes the underlying computation (re-reading sources, re-running transformations) unless you explicitly cache the DataFrame.
Global temp views live in the shared `global_temp` database backed by the SparkContext, so any SparkSession created from the same context (e.g., via newSession()) can resolve `global_temp.<name>`.

Session temp views disappear when the SparkSession ends; global temp views disappear when the SparkApplication / SparkContext terminates -- neither is written to the Hive metastore, so they are absent on restart.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame (logical plan) -> [createOrReplaceTempView -> SessionCatalog temp map] OR [createGlobalTempView -> global_temp DB on SparkContext] -> spark.sql(name) resolves name to plan -> Catalyst optimizes combined plan -> Execution (recomputes each query unless cached)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You build `df = spark.read.parquet(...).filter(...)` -- a logical plan, nothing executed yet.
2. `df.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")` stores that plan in the session catalog under `orders`.
3. `spark.sql("SELECT region, sum(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region")` inlines the `orders` plan and adds the aggregation.
4. Catalyst optimizes the whole thing (e.g., pushing the filter, pruning columns) and executes, reading Parquet at this point.
5. Running another query on `orders` re-executes the read+filter again, because the view is not materialized.

keyTerminology.meaning: A temporary view visible only within the SparkSession that created it (createOrReplaceTempView).
keyTerminology.importance: Prevents cross-session name clashes but means the view is unavailable to other sessions and dies with the session.

keyTerminology.meaning: A view stored in the reserved global_temp database, shareable across sessions of the same application.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables sharing across sessions but requires the global_temp.<name> qualifier and lives until the application ends.

keyTerminology.meaning: The view stores a logical plan, not data, so it is recomputed on each query unless the DataFrame is cached.
keyTerminology.importance: Avoids storage cost but can repeat expensive computation; cache when a view is queried many times.

keyTerminology.meaning: A reserved database name that holds all global temporary views.
keyTerminology.importance: All global temp views must be referenced as global_temp.<name>; the database name is configurable but reserved.

importantConcepts.concept: Views are query definitions, not tables
importantConcepts.explanation: A temporary view holds the DataFrame's logical plan, so it is re-evaluated every time it is queried. It is not a snapshot or a stored table. If you need a stable, reusable result, persist it (write to a table) or `cache()`/`persist()` the DataFrame before registering the view.

Session views are referenced by unqualified name and are private to a session; global views must be referenced as `global_temp.<name>` and are shared across sessions. A session view and a global view can share the same short name without conflict because they live in different catalogs.

`createOrReplaceTempView` overwrites an existing session view of the same name. `createGlobalTempView` throws AnalysisException if the global view already exists; use `createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` to overwrite. Choose the create-or-replace variants in idempotent pipelines.

variationsAndTypes: **createOrReplaceTempView:** Session-scoped, idempotently overwrites an existing same-named session view.
**createTempView:** Session-scoped but throws if the name already exists (no overwrite).
**createGlobalTempView:** Application-scoped under global_temp; throws on existing name.
**createOrReplaceGlobalTempView:** Application-scoped under global_temp; overwrites an existing global view.
**Cached view:** A view over a DataFrame that has been cache()/persist()ed, so repeated queries reuse materialized results.
advantages: **SQL + DataFrame interop:** Query DataFrames with full Spark SQL and mix styles freely.
**No storage cost:** Views store only a logical plan; nothing is written to disk or the metastore.
**Full optimization:** Catalyst optimizes the inlined view plan together with the surrounding query.
**Flexible scoping:** Session views isolate work; global views enable controlled cross-session sharing.
disadvantages: **Recomputation:** Non-materialized views recompute on every query, which can be expensive.
**Ephemeral:** Views vanish when the session (or application, for global) ends -- not persisted across restarts.
**Qualifier friction:** Global views require the global_temp.<name> prefix, an easy thing to forget.
**Not visible externally:** Other applications/tools cannot see temporary views; they are in-memory catalog entries only.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use temporary views to express transformations in SQL, to share an intermediate result across SQL steps in a session, and (global) to share an intermediate across multiple sessions in one application -- when no durable persistence is needed.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid relying on temporary views for results that must survive a session/application restart (use a managed/external table instead), and avoid re-querying a heavy view repeatedly without caching, which silently recomputes upstream work.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A temporary view is like a saved search or a smart playlist rather than a downloaded folder of files. The saved search (session temp view) is private to your account/session; a shared saved search (global temp view) is visible to your whole team within the same workspace. Either way, it re-runs the search each time you open it -- it stores the query, not a frozen copy of the results -- and it disappears when you log out (session) or the workspace closes (application).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A temporary view materializes/caches the data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It only stores the logical plan and is recomputed on each query. To materialize, you must cache()/persist() the DataFrame or write it to a table.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A global temp view can be queried by its short name like a session view.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Global temp views live in the global_temp database and must be referenced as global_temp.<name>; the unqualified name will not resolve.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Temporary views persist in the Hive metastore and survive restarts.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are in-memory catalog entries tied to the session (or application); they are never written to the metastore and are gone after the session/application ends.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Views add no storage, but repeated queries against a heavy non-materialized view recompute the upstream DAG each time; cache the underlying DataFrame when a view backs many queries to avoid redundant work at scale.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Lifecycle bugs (view gone after a session ends, or a global name clash) cause failures; prefer createOrReplace variants for idempotency and qualify global views correctly to avoid resolution errors.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: A view holds a recomputable plan, so on task/executor failure Spark simply re-executes from the source; there is no view state to lose because nothing is materialized.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch the Spark UI for repeated identical stages indicating a heavy view being recomputed across queries; this is a signal to cache. Use spark.catalog.listTables to audit registered temp views.
productionConsiderations.security: Temporary views inherit the permissions of the underlying data; global temp views widen visibility to all sessions in the application, so avoid placing sensitive intermediates in global_temp unless that sharing is intended.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Cache the backing DataFrame when a view is queried multiple times to convert repeated compute into a one-time materialization; drop unused views to keep the catalog clean (minor but avoids confusion).
productionConsiderations.performance: Because Catalyst inlines and re-optimizes the view plan per query, performance equals writing the query inline; the main lever is caching to avoid recomputation, plus standard predicate pushdown and pruning.

codeExamples.title: Session temp view: register and query with spark.sql
codeExamples.overview: Create a session-scoped temporary view and query it with SQL.
codeExamples.code:
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("east", 100), ("west", 250), ("east", 75)],
    ["region", "amount"])

# Session-scoped view (overwrites if it already exists)
df.createOrReplaceTempView("sales")

# Query it with SQL by its UNqualified name
result = spark.sql("""
    SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY region
    ORDER BY total DESC
""")
result.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: `createOrReplaceTempView('sales')` stores df's logical plan in the session catalog. `spark.sql(...)` resolves the unqualified name `sales` to that plan and runs the aggregation. Nothing was written; the underlying createDataFrame plan is inlined and optimized with the GROUP BY.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Trying to use the view from a different SparkSession (it will not be found); assuming the data is cached when it is only a plan reference.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you will query `sales` many times, call `df.cache()` (and trigger an action) before registering so repeated SQL queries reuse materialized data.

codeExamples.title: Global temp view: sharing across sessions
codeExamples.overview: Create a global temporary view and query it from a new session using the global_temp qualifier.
codeExamples.code:
df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Alice"), (2, "Bob")], ["id", "name"])

# Application-scoped view in the reserved global_temp database
df.createGlobalTempView("people_g")

# Must qualify with global_temp.<name>
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM global_temp.people_g").show()

# A NEW session (same SparkContext) can also see it
spark2 = spark.newSession()
spark2.sql("SELECT count(*) AS c FROM global_temp.people_g").show()

# Unqualified name does NOT resolve (this would error):
# spark.sql("SELECT * FROM people_g")  # AnalysisException
codeExamples.breakdown: `createGlobalTempView('people_g')` registers the view under `global_temp`. It is queried as `global_temp.people_g`. A second session created via `spark.newSession()` shares the SparkContext and can therefore see the same global view, demonstrating cross-session scope.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: First query lists Alice and Bob; second session returns c=2. Referencing the unqualified `people_g` raises an AnalysisException (table or view not found).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting the `global_temp.` prefix; calling createGlobalTempView twice with the same name raises an error -- use createOrReplaceGlobalTempView to overwrite.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Only promote to a global view when cross-session sharing is truly needed; session views avoid the qualifier and reduce name-collision risk.

codeExamples.title: Views are lazy: proving recomputation and fixing with cache
codeExamples.overview: Show that a view recomputes its underlying plan on each query and how caching avoids it.
codeExamples.code:
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

# Expensive-ish source plan (filter + derived column)
base = (spark.range(0, 1_000_000)
        .withColumn("sq", F.col("id") * F.col("id"))
        .filter(F.col("id") % 7 == 0))

base.createOrReplaceTempView("v")

# Each of these RE-RUNS the range+withColumn+filter (not materialized)
spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM v").show()
spark.sql("SELECT max(sq) FROM v").show()

# Cache the backing DataFrame, then re-register the view over it
base.cache().count()                 # materialize once
base.createOrReplaceTempView("v")
spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM v").show()  # now reads from cache

# Lifecycle: drop the view when done
spark.catalog.dropTempView("v")
codeExamples.breakdown: Each `spark.sql` on `v` re-executes the underlying range/withColumn/filter because the view is just a plan. After `base.cache().count()` materializes the result, subsequent queries reuse the cache. `dropTempView` removes the catalog entry, illustrating lifecycle management.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Counts/maxes are correct (e.g., count of multiples of 7 below 1,000,000). In the Spark UI, the first two queries show the full source stages; the post-cache query reads from the in-memory cache (InMemoryTableScan).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming the view caches automatically; caching the DataFrame but querying a view registered over the pre-cache plan (re-register after caching to be safe).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Cache the backing DataFrame once for views read many times; drop temporary views you no longer need to keep the catalog clean.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data team runs an interactive analytics application where multiple notebook sessions need to query the same cleaned, derived 'active customers' dataset using SQL, without each session re-deriving it from raw events and without persisting a physical table.
endToEndExample.inputData: A raw events DataFrame `events(customer_id, event_type, ts)` read from Parquet; the derived dataset is active customers (those with a 'purchase' event in the last 30 days) with their last activity timestamp.
endToEndExample.architecture: One Spark application hosts multiple sessions. A setup routine derives the active-customers DataFrame, caches it, and exposes it as a GLOBAL temporary view so every session can query it with SQL via spark.sql.
processingSteps: 1. Read raw `events` and derive `active = events.filter(purchase & last 30 days).groupBy('customer_id').agg(max('ts'))`.
2. `active.cache()` and trigger an action so the derived result is materialized once.
3. `active.createOrReplaceGlobalTempView('active_customers')` to share it across sessions idempotently.
4. Analyst session A: `spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM global_temp.active_customers")`.
5. Analyst session B (spark.newSession()): `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM global_temp.active_customers WHERE ...")`.
6. On shutdown, the global view and cache are released when the application ends (or drop explicitly).
endToEndExample.output: A globally shared, SQL-queryable `active_customers` view that all sessions read consistently, backed by a single cached materialization rather than per-session recomputation.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Check the Spark UI to confirm sessions read from the in-memory cache (InMemoryTableScan) rather than recomputing the derivation; use spark.catalog to verify the global view exists in global_temp.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Use createOrReplaceGlobalTempView so re-running setup does not throw on an existing name; sessions must qualify with global_temp. and handle AnalysisException if the application/cache was reset. If the application restarts, the view is gone -- re-run setup since temp views do not persist.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Multiple sessions share one cached, SQL-accessible derived dataset with no physical table to manage, balancing convenient SQL access and cross-session sharing against the understanding that the view is ephemeral and must be re-created per application lifetime.

industryUseCases.problem: Analysts want to query Spark DataFrames using familiar SQL within a notebook session.
industryUseCases.solution: Register DataFrames as session temp views with createOrReplaceTempView and query via spark.sql, mixing SQL and DataFrame steps.
industryUseCases.benefits: Frictionless SQL access to in-memory data, no table management, and full Catalyst optimization of the combined query.

industryUseCases.problem: Several sessions in one long-running application must share a common derived dataset.
industryUseCases.solution: Expose the derived DataFrame as a global temp view (createOrReplaceGlobalTempView) and query it as global_temp.<name> from each session.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent shared intermediate across sessions without persisting a physical table, with caching to avoid recomputation.

industryUseCases.company: ETL pipelines mixing SQL and DataFrame logic
industryUseCases.problem: Some transformation steps are clearer as SQL while others are DataFrame code.
industryUseCases.solution: Register intermediate DataFrames as temp views and express specific steps in SQL via spark.sql, then continue in the DataFrame API.
industryUseCases.benefits: Best-of-both-worlds expressiveness with zero intermediate storage, since views are just logical-plan references.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Temp views consume no storage, but the non-materialized nature means heavy views recompute per query. At scale, cache the backing DataFrame so N queries cost one materialization instead of N full recomputations; monitor for repeated identical stages.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Because a view stores a recomputable logical plan, executor or task failures simply re-run from source -- there is no materialized view state to recover. Cached views recover by recomputing lost cache partitions.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Views are application/session-local in-memory catalog entries; they do not survive driver restarts. For HA scenarios that must outlast the application, persist to a managed/external table instead of relying on temporary views.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Temporary views are not part of the metastore and are absent after any restart, so DR plans must recreate them via setup code; treat the source data and derivation code as the recoverable artifacts, not the views.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Performance matches inlining the query, since Catalyst re-optimizes the combined plan; the primary optimization is caching the backing DataFrame for repeatedly queried views, plus standard predicate pushdown and column pruning that flow through the inlined plan.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Avoid silent recomputation costs by caching views read multiple times and unpersisting when done. There is no storage cost for the view itself, so the only spend lever is compute reuse via caching.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Global temp views broaden visibility to every session in the application; do not register sensitive intermediates globally unless intended. Views inherit underlying data access controls and do not add a new persistence surface to secure.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use spark.catalog.listTables() and listTables('global_temp') to audit registered views; in the Spark UI, repeated full-scan stages for the same view signal a missing cache. Track view creation/drops in pipeline logs.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Since a view re-evaluates its plan, it always reflects the current definition of the source DataFrame; validate the underlying DataFrame's quality. When caching, ensure the cache was materialized after the data was finalized to avoid stale assumptions.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log view registration, scope (session vs global), and drops; alert on AnalysisExceptions for unqualified global views or name collisions (createGlobalTempView on an existing name) to catch lifecycle/scope bugs early.

recommendedPractices: **Use createOrReplaceTempView for idempotent session views** and createOrReplaceGlobalTempView for global ones to avoid errors on re-run.
**Cache the backing DataFrame** when a view backs many queries, since views are non-materialized and otherwise recompute each time.
**Always qualify global views** as `global_temp.<name>` in SQL.
**Prefer session scope by default** and promote to global only when cross-session sharing is genuinely required.
engineeringStandards: Drop temporary views you no longer need (dropTempView/dropGlobalTempView) to keep the catalog clean and avoid confusion.
Do not rely on temporary views for results that must survive a session/application restart -- persist to a table instead.
Re-register a view over a DataFrame after caching it so queries hit the cached plan.
designRecommendations: Use temp views to mix SQL and DataFrame steps where each is clearest, treating views as named, reusable query fragments.
Keep sensitive intermediate data out of global_temp unless application-wide sharing is intended.
For repeatedly shared, derived datasets, combine a cached DataFrame with a global view in the application setup.
namingConventions: Name views to reflect their content and scope, e.g., `active_customers` (session) and a clear global name registered under global_temp.
Avoid reusing the same short name for unrelated session and global views to prevent confusion, even though they live in separate catalogs.
documentationStandards: Document each view's scope (session vs global), whether it is cached, and its lifecycle/cleanup.
Record the qualifier requirement (global_temp.) for any global views in shared application code.
Note that temporary views are ephemeral and must be recreated by setup code on restart.
testingStrategies: Unit-test that querying a view returns the same result as the equivalent DataFrame operation.
Test scope behavior: a session view is invisible to another session, and a global view is visible across sessions of the same context.
Verify lifecycle: dropping a view removes it from the catalog and that re-create-or-replace is idempotent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a temporary view materializes/caches the data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The view behaves like a table in SQL, so engineers assume the data is stored once.
commonMistakes.impact: Every query recomputes the underlying plan, repeating expensive reads and transformations and inflating runtime/cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Treat a view as a query definition; cache()/persist() the backing DataFrame (and re-register the view) when it is queried multiple times.

commonMistakes.mistake: Querying a global temp view without the global_temp qualifier.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers expect to reference it by its short name like a session view.
commonMistakes.impact: Spark raises an AnalysisException (table or view not found), breaking the query.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reference global temp views as `global_temp.<name>` in SQL; only session views use the unqualified name.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting temporary views to persist across sessions or restarts.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: They look like tables and appear in the catalog, so people assume durability.
commonMistakes.impact: The view vanishes when the session (or application, for global) ends, causing 'not found' failures on the next run.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a managed/external table for durable results; recreate temp views via setup code each session/application as needed.

comparisonSection.explanation: A session view is visible only within the SparkSession that created it and is referenced by its unqualified name. A global view lives in the reserved global_temp database, is visible to all SparkSessions sharing the SparkContext, and must be referenced as global_temp.<name>.

A session view exists for the lifetime of its SparkSession and disappears when that session ends. A global temp view exists for the lifetime of the SparkApplication/SparkContext and is shared until the application terminates; neither persists to the metastore.

A temporary view stores only a logical plan and recomputes on each query, with no storage and no durability across restarts. A managed/external table physically persists data and survives restarts, but incurs storage cost and write I/O.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a temporary view in PySpark and how do you query it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is a named reference to a DataFrame's logical plan that you can query with SQL. You register it with `df.createOrReplaceTempView('name')` and query it via `spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM name')`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Confirms the basic mechanism of bridging the DataFrame and SQL APIs without writing data.

beginnerQuestions.question: Does creating a temporary view write any data to disk?
beginnerQuestions.answer: No. It stores only the DataFrame's logical plan in the in-memory catalog; no data is written and nothing is added to the Hive metastore.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding that views are non-materialized query definitions.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between createOrReplaceTempView and createGlobalTempView?
intermediateQuestions.answer: createOrReplaceTempView creates a session-scoped view visible only to the creating SparkSession, referenced by its unqualified name. createGlobalTempView creates an application-scoped view in the global_temp database, visible to all sessions sharing the SparkContext, referenced as global_temp.<name>.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The core scoping question; the answer must mention the global_temp qualifier and cross-session sharing.

intermediateQuestions.question: Are temporary views materialized? What happens when you query one twice?
intermediateQuestions.answer: They are not materialized -- they store a logical plan. Querying twice recomputes the underlying plan both times unless you cache()/persist() the backing DataFrame.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests awareness of laziness and the caching remedy for repeated queries.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the lifecycle of a session vs a global temporary view?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A session view lives as long as its SparkSession and disappears when the session ends. A global view lives as long as the SparkApplication/SparkContext. Neither persists to the metastore or survives a restart.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Checks understanding that views are ephemeral and tied to session/application lifecycle.

advancedQuestions.question: How does Spark internally resolve and optimize a query against a temporary view?
advancedQuestions.answer: The view's logical plan is stored in the SessionCatalog (or global_temp for global views). When spark.sql references the name, Spark substitutes the view's logical plan inline, then Catalyst optimizes the combined plan (predicate pushdown, pruning, etc.) as if the query were written without the view -- so performance equals inlining.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates knowledge of catalog resolution and that views are an optimization-transparent abstraction.

advancedQuestions.question: When would you choose a cached temp view over writing an intermediate table?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use a cached temp view when the intermediate is needed only within the current application lifetime and you want fast SQL access without storage/write I/O. Write a table when the result must persist across restarts, be shared with external tools, or be too large to cache reliably.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests trade-off reasoning between ephemeral caching and durable persistence.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Two analysts in the same Spark application need to query the same derived dataset via SQL, but one analyst's session cannot see the view the other registered. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: A view registered with createOrReplaceTempView is session-scoped, so it is invisible to other sessions. To share across sessions in one application, use a global temp view and reference it with the global_temp qualifier.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Register the dataset with createOrReplaceGlobalTempView and have both sessions query it as global_temp.<name>. Optionally cache the backing DataFrame so both sessions reuse one materialization instead of recomputing.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an interactive analytics service where many sessions query a common derived dataset via SQL efficiently, without a persistent table.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: In application setup, derive the dataset, cache() it and trigger materialization, then expose it via createOrReplaceGlobalTempView. Sessions query global_temp.<name>. Recreate on application restart since views are ephemeral.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Global views enable cross-session sharing but require the qualifier and broaden visibility; caching trades memory for avoiding recomputation; choosing temp views over a table avoids storage but sacrifices durability.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Cache once to serve many sessions, size executor memory for the cached dataset, monitor the UI for cache hits vs recomputation, and fall back to a materialized table if the dataset is too large to cache or must persist.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A temporary view is a non-materialized, named logical-plan reference queryable via spark.sql; createOrReplaceTempView is session-scoped while createGlobalTempView is application-scoped under global_temp.

Global view: global_temp.<name>, shared across sessions of the application.

keyTakeaways: A temporary view is a named, non-materialized reference to a DataFrame's logical plan that you query with spark.sql; it stores the query definition, not the data, so it is recomputed on each query unless the backing DataFrame is cached.

createOrReplaceTempView is session-scoped (visible only to its SparkSession, referenced by unqualified name), while createGlobalTempView is application-scoped in the reserved global_temp database (shared across sessions, referenced as global_temp.<name>).

Temporary views are ephemeral and tied to the SparkSession (session views) or SparkApplication/SparkContext (global views); they are never written to the metastore and disappear on restart, so use a table for durable results.
createOrReplace variants overwrite idempotently, whereas createGlobalTempView throws on an existing name; always reference global views with the global_temp qualifier to avoid AnalysisExceptions.
Cache the backing DataFrame for views queried many times to avoid silent recomputation, and drop views you no longer need to keep the catalog clean.
